packs.title: Gardens, Art and County Stories
packs.promise: Explore Fresno through admitted gardens, museums, zoo spaces and public street architecture.

q.s: Collect design clues from a real zoo viewing area.
st: Choose one open ordinary animal-exhibit viewing area. Read the current sign to establish which habitat or animal area you are observing; an animal does not need to be visible.
Find three distinct design clues: something separating visitors from the animal area, something shaping the habitat space, and something that helps visitors understand or view it.
Record where each feature sits and what its visible or labelled role is. Separate a role supported by a sign from an interpretation of your own; do not guess animal welfare or behaviour.

q.s: Follow one visual question across two available artworks.
st: Choose one available work and read its label. Pick one visible quality to investigate: repeated marks, the relationship of a figure to its setting, or how a strong edge directs your eye.
Find a second available work that lets you examine the same quality differently. Record the title or identifying label of each; do not attribute a medium or intention without evidence.
Write a comparison with one precise observation from each work and one difference. Keep the focus on what you can support from the objects and their current labels.

q.s: Turn a real experiment into an original instruction card.
st: Read the Wind Tunnel instructions and choose only an object or setup provided for ordinary visitor use. Predict what it will do before using the controls.
Try the permitted experiment, keeping hands and objects in the instructed positions. Observe one actual change in motion; stop if staff or a closure sign prevents use.

Create your own three-step instruction card or three labelled sketches for repeating that same permitted experiment. Add a sentence explaining how the observed result differed from or matched your prediction.

packs.title: Civic Corners and Fulton Art
packs.promise: Explore the connected downtown streets through public exterior landmarks, art, movement and a park pause.

q.s: Reduce an actual civic exterior to a small original drawing.
st: Choose a stopped public viewpoint that shows several exterior forms without entering the building. Pick five major lines or edges that would help someone recognize your view.
Make a five-line drawing, or write five short shape descriptions. Use only the actual visible exterior; no architect’s intention or historical interpretation is required.
Add one small original detail or label to distinguish your drawing from a generic building. Keep that detail visible from the same public viewpoint.

q.s: Collect form clues from a specific street sculpture.
st: Identify Aquarius Ovoid from its actual form and the source's stated block. Choose a safe stopped position where you can see its outer shape.
Find three different form details: a broad outline, a space or opening within or around the form, and a support or surface change. Describe what you can actually see; running water is not required.
Draw those relationships or write a three-part description that would distinguish this sculpture from the nearby tile benches. Do not guess what a hidden mechanism does.

q.s: Make an original exterior composition beside Fulton.
st: Choose a public sidewalk view and identify three different large exterior shapes or repeated groupings you can actually see. A roof edge, vertical run and doorway outline are examples, not promised details.
Arrange those forms into a small original drawing or four-line written composition. Change their scale on your page to emphasize the relationship you noticed.
Add one visible detail that makes your work specific to this building, then check that you have not invented an interior or described a private view.
